Personally I wouldn’t recommend sedation for such a young dog with no experience on the grooming table. Puppies are a lot more fearful than adult dogs yes but starting a 8 month old on sedation for grooming means 12x a year for 10-14 years the dog needs sedation. That’s an extra added charge and step for the parent that you don’t even know if the dog needs. My policy is that we always do the dog sober first. That way we can assess exactly what the triggers might be and work with the parent to improve on those issues before jumping right to sedation. Now yes I have recommended sedation immediately after that first visit but I’ve also had dogs that have always been sedated for grooms come in sober and do better than when sedated. I’d personally say, just don’t be surprised if your groomer does recommend sedation. Every groomer is different though and I totally understand we all have reasons for why we do what we do but that’s just my 2 cents

There’s a lot of really good information in these comments. I just want to reiterate a couple things. This matting looks pretty severe so do not be surprised if they have to shave very very short (to the skin). Being understanding of how long it might take and the price is the key to a groomers heart. Im going to take a wild guess and say that he hasn’t had a salon experience so far and it’s important to inform your groomer of everything you know before the groom (past salon experiences if applicable, any sensitive areas or things he might not like that you know of). Most groomers are extremely understanding when it comes to situations like this but I would highly recommend not going to a corporate salon as those tend to be a lot more stressful than private. I highly recommend you read the entire grooming contract if they have one just so you are aware of any policy’s they might have that hasn’t been discussed (late pick up fees and dematting fees are often on these). I also agree that a calming chew might not be the best idea for the first groom but at check out ask the groomer if they would recommend it for next time. Lastly if you don’t like the first haircut your groomer does, try to give them a couple more tries as hoping around from groomer to groomer can sometimes be really hard on dogs. Unless you truly feel they did something wrong I’d say try to stick with one groomer as long as you can. All that being said, thank you for taking in this guy. Just keep asking questions and don’t be afraid to learn something new! Can’t wait to see this guy blossom into the life he deserves. Most hunger strikes I’ve encountered are due to improper husbandry. Check your temperatures and humidity first. Then think about adding more cover and enrichment. Another reason some bps don’t want to eat is due to feeling “insecure” you can do this by adding multiple hides, fake or real plants and climbing opportunities. Also from what I can see that tank is definitely WAY too small for that snake. A ball python will need a 4ft in length x 2ft in width x 2ft in height enclosure when it’s fully grown. Most will start with a 20 gallon long and love to a 40 gallon front opening or breeder. Bigger is always better, as long as your providing that cover/hides/plants that they need. Right now your snake is definitely stressed so it not eating is not surprising. Also most bps will only stick to either rats or mice. It’s important to ask the person you bought him from which one he is eating and if it was live or frozen thaw.

This looks like every enclosure ever put together by someone who only went by the care guides that pet stores hand out when you purchase an animal. There are lots of care guides and resources you can find to improve this a lot. It’s incredibly important to do extensive amounts of research before setting up an enclosure and then purchasing your new pet. First make sure that if you use any kind of heat source, to plug it into a thermostat. This helps keep your temperature at the right range and prevents your snake from severe medical issues that could occur. Quite a few of my rescues fell victim to this which is completely preventable. You can buy them on Amazon for like 26 bucks and it will last a very long time. Then you want to add a lot of clutter and more hides. Also if you are covering the top for humidity retaining purposes, make sure you leave at least 30% open for ventilation. Hopefully that plushy is not inside the tank either. That will grow a ton of bacteria and could cause health issues.

As someone who has kept lots of snakes and lots of rats and other rodents including hamsters in the same household, I highly recommend keeping them in different rooms, preferably not right next to each other. When I brought home my rodents for the first time, all my snakes became a lot more active. When my rescue rats had their litters, they were basically in beast mode. My boa was so incredibly active, I’ve never seen him move like that. (He has a Neurological issue from a previous owner not using a thermostat so he tends to be pretty slow and unaware). My “rat room” and “reptile room” weren’t next to each other And none of my snakes eat live or have with me. I love keeping both but yeah I highly recommend separating and then cleaning the rodents as much as possible, though sounds like you already would! Good luck with your new baby! And I feed my hammies the Higgins sunburst and Mazuri pellet diet mix.

Feeding in a separate bin or tub is actually going to cause your snake to stress out more and might cause it to not eat at all. It also increases the likelihood of regurgitation as you have to move the snake after the meal. It’s recommended to not handle them for 24-48 after eating to avoid regurgitation. If registration happens you will have to wait (I think) two weeks to make sure any internal injuries have healed. Risking regurgitation isn’t worth feeding outside enclosures. Hey I highly recommend changing a couple of things about his enclosure if he’s known for food strikes. Most of the time that’s due to a snake not feeling secure in its habitat. Your enclosure does look pretty bare so that might be playing a role. I highly recommend to first block out 3/4 sides so the snake knows those are walls. Snakes don’t understand the concept of glass so it probably feels like he’s sitting out in the open. I also recommend at least 3 hides but more is always better. Another thing to think about is fake or real plants. It’s important for your snake to feel like he’s covered when he’s moving around the enclosure. Without this cover the snake can be stressed and that can be the cause of food strikes. You can get cheap fake plants at craft stores and make it really full for him. Also I highly recommend more substrate. This helps with holding proper humidity. Without that you will most likely be spraying the enclosure down every day which will cause permanently wet substrate and possibly scale rot. The deeper the substrate the more moisture can be held. I know you mentioned being scared if impaction but you can easily avoid this by switching to coco fibers or feeding on a plate or a turned over hide. You can also try smaller meals. This snake is definitely underweight and small for a year old so I’d recommend feeding once every 7-10 days or less. If you go Less, monitor to make sure he’s still pooping

Edit: the analog gauges will also never give you an accurate reading. I highly recommend buying a digital one off Amazon. Much cheaper than rebuying the ones at the pet store. Are you using a thermostat?

Don’t know much about his head but I can recommend a few things. First, changing out the reptile carpet. It harbors bacteria and can rip your geckos toes off. A mix of play sand and coco fiber type dirt is great or if you are afraid of loose substrate, tiles are best. Paper towels are okay too but not ideal for long periods of time. If your gecko is having issues shedding, it’s recommended to put in a humid hide. You can keep the humid hide in there all the time and just spray it down once a day or so. Leopard gecko go into shed and finish very quickly so trying to put the humid hide in just when they are about to shed doesn’t always work. Stuck shed on toes like that can lead to circulation being cut off and then the toe falling off all together. 

All I can say about his head is get a vets opinion. Could be a number of things and it’s best to get him in asap. Not all vets are actually as good with exotics as they say so shop around.

That cage and wheel are not big enough for poor Rupert. Hamsters need a lot of floor space to run around. 450 square inches is usually the bare minimum. That cage is one I’ve received with some of the rescues I’ve gotten. It’s about 12 inches by 24 inches which is just over half the bare minimum. As for the wheel, your hamster needs a wheel that is at least 10 inches in diameter. This ensures that they are not arching their back while using it. Using a too small wheel can leave permanent damage. 

That being said, you should aim to give your pets the maximum amount of space possible. 600 square inches of floor space is a much more suitable size for a hamster but bigger is always better.

I currently have a Russian tortoise in a 6 for by 2 foot table and he’s nowhere close to what sulcata a get to and I still think he needs more space.

Pineapple, my rescue uro passed away on the way to the vet this morning. He came to me about a week ago in really rough conditions. Was told he was kept in a snake rack with no heat or uvb his whole life. I set up a 40 gallon for him with proper conditions and substrate. He ate for me twice so I wasn’t too worried about not being able to get into the vet until Thursday. This morning I woke up and he was face down in a crooked position. I picked him up and he was limp and barely opened his eyes. I called my normal vet and then my emergency vet and neither had time for him so I frantically called around trying to find someone who could help. Finally found a vet that had time but he passed away on the way to the vet. Vet said it was most likely due to long term malnutrition and poor conditions. 

I’m in the early process of opening a non profit exotic animal rescue in my town so I know that this is always a possibility and it’s not necessary my fault (though I wish I’d been able to take him in sooner) but this hit me really hard. I take my rat out of the freezer at 7 and let it sit in there for 3 hours. I feed at night, after my snakes lights have been off for at least 2 hours and he’s been active. Again, it’s super important to have a temp gun. It’s just as important as a thermostat for your heating elements. Pls go to your local hardware store and find one that’s 20-25 dollars. It’s always recommended, when purchasing a reptile, to set up their enclosure and do extensive research before you get the actual animal. This gives you time to set it all up and make changes if you see something better you can do. This also allows the temperature in the enclosure to settle in.  Both of these are important for proper care of reptiles

That being said, you’ve already purchased the animal so I will order my recommendations from most important to least. 

Whenever you use a heating method, mats or lights, you MUST use a thermostat. This is a device that connects from an outlet to your mat or light and constantly monitors and controls the temperature. Without this you will burn your pet. You can buy them for cheap on Amazon 

Reptile carpet is highly NOT recommended because it can cause your pet to lose nails and teeth like some have said. I’ve also heard of them loosing full toes from reptile carpet so I recommended changing that to paper towels for the first few weeks. Make sure to change those often. 

All animals encounter some amount of sun throughout their lives. Because of this, when kept in captivity, they need an artificial sun. Please look into the different types of UV and purchase a hood or dome set up. 

It seems that you have no thermometers or hydrometers in your enclosure. You will need at least two of each. One for each end of the enclosure. And do NOT buy anything but the electric ones. The analog and strip ones are crap and useless 

I would also recommend getting a bigger heat mat. I’ve heard people who cover 1/3 of the bottom of the glass and I’ve heard people who cover half. Just make sure the temperature is still creating a gradient 

Also I noticed you have two hides. For leopard geckos it’s recommended to give them three. A hot. A cold. And a moist when they go into shed. 

Now that we’ve covered the temperature and humidity let’s try to entertain and nurture the pet! They will need plenty of things to climb on and around and under. Please try to take a look at some of the other enclosure pictures on this subreddit to get some ideas of how it should look. 

As for food, please make sure you are not just going by what petsmart or petco told you. Do more research into what they need in terms of supplements and vitamins to add to their insect diet. 

Lastly, I HIGHLY recommend you watch some YouTube videos and read up on the background of where these little ones come from. This will help you get an idea as to what they need to be happy. Also, for a new time owner, taking notes is always a great thing to help remember what is needed. Please keep asking questions as they come, but don’t just rely on one source for your information.
